1. Core Clinical Tension: An 82-year-old immigrant woman presents initially with subacute fever, dry cough, and constitutional decline initially misdiagnosed as community-acquired pneumonia, only to return one month later in overt New York Heart Association Class III heart failure with cardiac tamponade. Advanced thoracic imaging reveals not only a massive 37 mm circumferential pericardial effusion with pericardial thickening, but also ipsilateral basal micronodular infiltrates and two distinct pulmonary nodules (up to 22 mm). This clinical picture creates a crucial diagnostic tension between metastatic bronchogenic carcinoma, pyogenic bacterial/fungal pericarditis, and extrapulmonary granulomatous mycobacterial pericarditis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is reached upon her emergency admission for acute cardiac tamponade, following chest radiography, thoracic computed tomography, and transthoracic echocardiography documenting the effusion and lung nodules, but immediately prior to emergency pericardiocentesis, pericardial fluid biochemical/cytologic analysis, and send-out mycobacterial PCR and cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Common bacterial or viral pneumonia can cause reactive effusions, but viral pericarditis is typically self-limited, and pyogenic pericarditis presents with hyperacute fulminant septic shock with purulent effusion. Metastatic adenocarcinoma of the lung frequently causes malignant pericardial effusions with pulmonary nodularity and thickened pericardial leaflets in elderly smokers or non-smokers, but cytologic examination and targeted molecular testing will show non-malignant lymphocytic exudate containing acid-fast organisms rather than neoplastic cells.
case_prompt:
An 82-year-old woman originally from Ukraine presented to the emergency department with a two-week history of low-grade fever, non-productive cough, generalized weakness, and anorexia. She denied night sweats or notable weight loss and had no significant prior medical illnesses or chronic medications. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3 °C, blood pressure of 105/71 mmHg, heart rate of 99 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 95% on ambient air. Cardiac auscultation demonstrated distinctly muffled heart sounds; pulmonary auscultation was clear bilaterally.

A plain chest radiograph showed an accentuated reticular pattern predominantly at the right pulmonary base and an enlarged cardiac silhouette with an increased cardiothoracic index. Electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm with low-voltage QRS complexes and diffuse flattened T waves. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 87.3 fL) and an elevated C-reactive protein of 57.6 mg/L (reference <= 5.0 mg/L). An initial diagnosis of atypical pneumonia was presumed, and she was discharged on oral antibacterial therapy.

At a one-month follow-up evaluation, her fever had abated, but she developed severe exertional dyspnea (NYHA Functional Class III). A repeat chest radiograph showed marked further enlargement of the cardiothoracic index. Thoracic computed tomography demonstrated micronodular opacities at the right lung base, two distinct solid pulmonary nodules (the larger measuring 22 mm in diameter), thickened pericardial leaflets, and a massive circumferential pericardial effusion. Emergency transthoracic echocardiography confirmed a massive circumferential pericardial effusion measuring up to 37 mm adjacent to the left heart chambers, accompanied by a 'swinging heart' sign and overt echocardiographic indicators of tamponade (diastolic collapse of the right heart chambers and pronounced respiratory variation in transvalvular inflow velocities). Serum cardiac troponin was normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Community-Acquired Pneumonia with Reactive Paraneoplastic or Viral Pericarditis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initially diagnosed and treated with broad-spectrum oral antibiotics based on dry cough, basal reticular markings, and elevated CRP, but ruled out when her cardiac status deteriorated over four weeks into overt cardiac tamponade with large pulmonary nodules on CT.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A diagnosis of pneumonia was assumed, and the patient was discharged with antibiotherapy.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the patient's elderly age, anorexia, subacute course, multiple right lung parenchymal nodules up to 22 mm, and a massive exudative effusion with thickened pericardial leaflets, but excluded when pericardial fluid cytology, bronchoscopic evaluation, and tissue biopsy showed epithelioid granulomatous inflammation rather than malignant cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A thoracic computed tomography described micronodular opacities on the right pulmonary base and two nodular formations, the larger measuring 22 mm (Figure 3). A large circumferential PE and thickened leaflets were also noted

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The definitive turning point occurred following pericardiocentesis yielding 1000 mL of exudative fluid (LDH 1599 U/L, protein ratio 9.6), where real-time polymerase chain reaction and mycological culture positively identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis, further corroborated by bronchoalveolar lavage PCR and endobronchial biopsy demonstrating caseating epithelioid granulomas.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: however, the mycologic culture was positive, and PCR allowed the identification of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MT).

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case following Stanford MedCaseReasoning. Breakpoint stops at the moment of cardiac tamponade diagnosis on echocardiography before pericardiocentesis and PCR results. Zero spoilers in case_prompt. Candidates and Diagnostic Pivot supported by verbatim quotes.
